newsitem.title: UK: British forces arrest 11 in anti-guerrilla swoop.
newsitem.headline: British forces arrest 11 in anti-guerrilla swoop.

text.p: British forces discovered a suspected IRA mortar and arrested 11 people in anti-guerrilla swoops in Belfast and Lurgan on Thursday, security sources said.
Gerry Adams, head of the Irish Republican Army's Sinn Fein political arm, earlier accused a soldier of firing a shot when he was stopped at a checkpoint. British army sources dismissed the charge.
The incidents happened as British and Irish ministers prepared for important talks in London on Northern Ireland's shattered peace process.
Security sources said a device found behind houses in Lurgan, 30 miles (50 km) south of Belfast, appeared to be a type used by IRA guerrillas who have intensified their battle against British rule.
"We have located a device which the army technical officer is still examining," police superintendent Neville McCoubrey told reporters."We believe it to be some sort of horizontal-type mortar."
If it had been fired at a target such as a British military vehicle "then death and injury would definitely have resulted," he said.
Around 100 homes were evacuated and a section of the cross-border Belfast to Dublin rail line at Lurgan was closed during the search operation.
The device was found after three men were detained in the early hours. Security sources said they had been acting suspiciously near Lurgan's railway station.
A bomb was later thrown at a security vehicle in the province but no one was injured.
Earlier in a separate crackdown on suspected IRA activities, eight people were arrested and several houses searched in Catholic nationalist areas of west Belfast.
A police patrol in Dungannon town narrowly escaped injury in what was thought to be an IRA bomb attack late on Wednesday.

Adams said a member of the locally-recruited and largely Protestant Royal Irish Regiment, which is part of the British Army, discharged a shot while he andSinn Fein colleague Gerry Kelly were held at a road checkpoint near Belfast.
A military source insisted Adams was mistaken. The patrol's weapons had been checked and not had been discharged, the source said.

In London Irish Deputy Prime Minister Dick Spring and Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew held their first talks of the year about the province's peace process,which is deadlocked and overshadowed by growing guerrilla violence.
Britain and Ireland says the IRA must abandon violence to win a place for Sinn Fein in peace talks. Sinn Fein says it should have immediate unconditional entry to talks.
